title: How can I solve the Meshy AI → Mixamo → Blender → 8-direction sprite sheet workflow problem?
author: AgeComfortable5104
selftext:
I know this isn’t really a Blender or Mixamo forum, but I thought I’d ask anyway in case someone here has run into the same problem before.

The main issue I’m running into is that the first imported animation works perfectly, but when I add additional Mixamo animations — for example, adding an Attack animation after Idle — the character no longer matches the original setup exactly.

When I import both animations into the same Blender scene and compare them, I can see that they are not perfectly aligned. Depending on the animation, the character may have a slightly different position, rotation, root transform, or base pose. In some cases the skeleton appears to be in the same general location, but the pose or bone transforms are different enough that the mesh does not overlap correctly.

This becomes a major problem when rendering 8-direction sprite sheets, because every animation needs to use the exact same character placement, scale, orientation, camera framing, and rotation center. Otherwise the character visibly shifts, rotates, or changes position between Idle, Walk, Attack, and other animations.

What is the proper workflow for importing and combining multiple Mixamo animations so that they all use the same existing rig and mesh, without introducing different transforms or rest poses? 

For example i rendered zombie\_idle  , zombie\_attack animation into one spirte png to see the issue.

comments.author: forrestwear
comments.body:
from how I understand it, you need to get meshy to make the rig, and then texture, and do NOT use any animations from meshy if you're going to use mixamo. meshy's fbx is all you need, and then only use animations from mixamo. 

mixamo auto rigs differently than meshy so that is why the textures are different sizes. 

now, you can use both, and just simply resize in blender/godot, but a lot of things can go wrong when importing. you can also retarget animations, and with a little web search, you'll understand what I mean.

typically, i'd only use meshy for making a model, and texturing, and then cleaning it up in blender, then importing  to mixamo, then exporting to your desired tool for game dev. 

all the stuff from the toplogyai sub is grift, so i'm not sure how the alternatives are. GL

comments.author: Mindestiny
comments.body:
This question gets asked here probably four times a day.  The answer is "whoever figures it out is gonna turn it into a webapp and make millions charging token rates for their frontend."

The tech just really isnt there to go from prompt to 3D to accurately rigged model to 8-direction spritesheets all in a click.  It's the right *idea* for a workflow but every single step's output needs manual cleanup still so the quality issues compound into mush by the end.

So doesnt matter what i do, all the animation have different stances, feet positions etc at beginning and never will blend. Maybe if i blend them manually.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
Yep, that pretty much sums it up.  Even non-AI based auto rigging is only a best guess and tends to not be quite right.  It'll get the rigging maybe 80% there on a very clear, normal adult human body but still requires some manual adjustment before you can accurately apply mocap to animate.  And then the mocap likely isn't great because you're applying a generalized mocap to a specific model (I.E. mocap made with a 5' 10" man will not look great on a model that doesn't perfectly align with a 5' 10" representation of a man with identical build and limb length).

If you're willing to clean up between each step, the workflow will save you time compared to hand making each part, but yeah.  It's not something you can fully end-to-end automate and have come out production quality at this time.  That's the kind of workflow that will revolutionize how AAA production assets get made.

replies.author: AgeComfortable5104
replies.body:
I understand. The rigging itself wouldn’t really be a problem for me, since this is an isometric 2D game with low-FPS sprite animations, so small rigging mistakes wouldn’t be very noticeable.

The real problem is that when Mixamo rigs a character and you download, say, three animations  idle, walk, and attack  the mesh/model ends up with a different pose or alignment in each one. The feet might be in a different position, the body posture changes, and so on. Because of that, the result looks terrible when I try to play the animations one after another. For example, if the character transitions from idle into an attack, there’s a visible “jump” because the body positions between the two animations are too different.

I was also thinking about using Blender MCP with Codex to create transitions between them, so that every animation either starts from the same idle pose or returns to the idle pose at the end.

Could that be a workable solution? I’m trying to build a workflow where I don’t have to spend days or weeks manually fixing every single character just to get three usable animations out of it.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body: It's worth a proof of concept, but as you point out it's not something you're going to be able to just feed into a start to finish automation pipeline.  You're gonna have to make those manual corrections for every single character, every single rig, every single attack animation.

comments.author: Suspicious_Neck_4069
comments.body:
My previous workflow using Unity:

1. Create the 3D model > export as FBX > rig using Mixamo or AccuRig (free and higher quality).

2. Import the rigged model > configure it in "Humanoid" mode.

3. Import all necessary animations from Mixamo.

4. Create an Animator mask to keep the leg position constant.

5. Add the animations to the Animator in Humanoid mode.

6. Take screenshots and assemble the spritesheet in Photoshop.
